Choosing a tree

MerkleForge ships three tree variants. They share the MerkleTree<H> trait but are built for different shapes of data.

BinaryMerkleTree<H>SparseMerkleTree<H>MerklePatriciaTrie<H>
Data shapeOrdered listMap from 32-byte keys to valuesMap from byte keys to values
Addressed byLeafIndex[u8; 32] key&[u8] key
ProofsInclusionMembership and non-membershipMembership and non-membership (RLP witness)
Proof size⌈log₂ n⌉ siblings256 siblings, empty ones compressed to NoneOne RLP node per trie level on the path
Best hashSha256 or Blake3Sha256 or Blake3Keccak256 for Ethereum roots
Typical useTransaction batches, logs, file chunks, SPVAccount state, rollups, allowlistsEthereum state, receipts, storage proofs

Quick decision guide

  • You have a list and prove items by position: use BinaryMerkleTree. It has the smallest proofs and the fastest construction.
  • You have a key-value map and need to prove a key is absent: use SparseMerkleTree. Keys are 32 bytes, so hash longer keys first.
  • You need roots or witnesses that Ethereum tooling understands: use MerklePatriciaTrie<Keccak256>.

Writing code that works with any variant

The shared trait lets you write generic code. Each variant also has a native API (keys for the sparse tree and trie); the trait maps leaf indices onto it.

use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::{BinaryMerkleTree, MerklePatriciaTrie, SparseMerkleTree};
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;
 
/// Insert rows through the shared trait and return a metadata snapshot.
fn commit<H, T>(tree: &mut T, rows: &[&[u8]]) -> Result<TreeMetadata, MerkleError>
where
    H: HashFunction,
    T: MerkleTree<H>,
{
    for row in rows {
        tree.insert(row)?;
    }
    Ok(tree.metadata())
}
 
fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let rows: &[&[u8]] = &[b"alice:100", b"bob:250", b"carol:75"];
 
    let binary = commit(&mut BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;
    let sparse = commit(&mut SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;
    let trie = commit(&mut MerklePatriciaTrie::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;
 
    for meta in [binary, sparse, trie] {
        println!("{:<18} leaves={} height={}", meta.variant, meta.leaf_count, meta.height);
    }
    Ok(())
}

How the trait maps onto each variant

  • Binary: insert appends and returns the next LeafIndex. remove replaces the leaf with H::empty(); later indices are unchanged.
  • Sparse: leaf index i is stored at a key whose last 8 bytes are i in big-endian order. insert returns the first unoccupied index at or above the leaf count, so it never overwrites a leaf after a removal. generate_proof returns a MerkleProof with 256 path nodes.
  • Patricia: leaf index i is stored under the key b"merkleforge:mpt:trait-leaf:" ‖ i (8 bytes, big-endian). generate_proof through the trait returns MerkleError::UnsupportedOperation, because Patricia proofs are key-addressed. Use MerklePatriciaTrie::generate_proof(key) instead.

Use the trait for generic plumbing (ingestion, metadata, benchmarks). Use each variant's native API when you need key-addressed proofs.
